additions.text: Śrīdhara Svāmī does not provide a separate explanatory block for this verse in the pinned Sanskrit file; the pinned Sanskrit Chapter 5 source ends at verse 50 although the pinned English mirror contains a record for 3.5.51.

The two verses connect as follows: perceiving Brahmā’s intention as he labored to understand the arrangement of the worlds, He spoke to him. His mind was despondent because of that water of dissolution. ‘Kaśmala’ means delusion. The word ‘iva’ indicates the complete pacification of all delusion.

The secondary creation of the gods is eightfold. Among it, the classes beginning with the vibudhas make three divisions; Gandharvas and Apsarases one; Yakṣas and Rākṣasas one; Bhūtas, Pretas and Piśācas one; Siddhas, Cāraṇas and Vidyādharas one; and Kinnaras and the rest one. By ‘and the rest’ are included Kimpuruṣas, horse-faced beings and so forth. This will be made clear in the twentieth chapter.

It is beneficial to the families of sages; ‘surodhasoḥ’ means having beautiful banks on both sides.

Anticipating the question ‘What is that Brahmāvarta?’ he says, ‘where there is the city named Barhiṣmatī.’ And where is that? Where the hairs of Yajña, the sacrificial Boar, fell. The word ‘where’ is to be connected throughout.

While explaining the derivation of the name Barhiṣmatī, in two verses he incidentally states the excellence of the country. There were kuśa and kāśa grasses. ‘Śaśvat’ means always; their appearance or color was permanently green. ‘Destroyers of sacrifice’ means Rākṣasas and the like. Having brought them to defeat, [the grasses protect] Yajña, Viṣṇu.
‘Greater than daiva’ means one who is capable of making even destiny otherwise. She had been made thin by observance of the vow; moreover, over a long period she had become extremely emaciated.
‘Upakaraṇa’ means equipment or surrounding furnishings. Paṭṭikās are particular silk cloths of small breadth; patākās are broad or extended ones; [the place was adorned] with these.
They had variegated garlands and flowers. The garlands were such that six-footed bees, humming and buzzing in a way that produced a sweet sound, were upon them.

The sage saw her again bearing that very form of her own which she had before the marriage. Her beautiful breasts were covered and clothed. On the alternative reading, the phrase indicates a particular feature of her form.
She had beautiful garments. Love had arisen in her. O destroyer of enemies—one who has conquered desire!

‘Yuktām’ means suitable or worthy. ‘Ayacchat’ means he gave [her].

He says in two verses beginning with ‘this’ that He grants liberation of this kind to exclusive devotees. ‘Ubhayāyinam’ means one who goes to both worlds; ‘the self’ means the self together with limiting adjuncts. ‘Those who follow the self’ are sons, wife and others, and also cattle and the like. ‘Rāyaḥ’ means wealth. ‘And other possessions’ continues the list. ‘I carry them beyond death’ means I take them completely across saṃsāra.
